title: Decimal Integer Palindrome Problem

content.problemStatement: The task is to output true when the base-10 representation of integer x reads the same in both directions; otherwise output false. Negative integers are not palindromes, and a positive integer ending in zero is not a palindrome.
constraints: Try to use O(1) extra space and avoid converting the number to a string for the follow-up.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialised return value (true or false)

sampleTestCases.explanation: The decimal representation "121" is identical when read from right to left, so the result is true.
Negative values include a minus sign and are not considered decimal palindromes. Therefore -121 returns false.
Reversing the digits of 10 would produce 01, which is not the same decimal representation. Therefore the result is false.

hidden.label: Largest possible palindrome with zeros inside

notes: All hidden test cases are concrete and use the documented JSON argument format.

solution.approach: Numeric half-reversal: reject negative numbers and numbers ending with 0 (except 0). Repeatedly pop digits from the end and build a reversed half. Stop when the original number is less than or equal to the reversed half. Compare the two halves (for odd-length numbers, discard the middle digit from the reversed half). This avoids string conversion and uses O(1) extra space.
notes: Negative integers are never considered palindromes.
Any positive integer ending with 0 (except 0 itself) is not a palindrome.
The follow-up encourages solving the problem without converting the integer into a string.
Reversing only half of the digits avoids overflow while maintaining O(1) extra space.

hints: Negative numbers are never palindromes because of the leading '-' sign.
If a positive number ends with 0, it cannot be a palindrome unless the number itself is 0.
Instead of reversing the entire number, reverse only half of its digits.
Stop reversing once the reversed half becomes greater than or equal to the remaining half.
For odd-length numbers, ignore the middle digit before comparing the two halves.
followUps: Can you solve the problem without converting the integer into a string?
Why is reversing only half of the digits safer than reversing the entire number?
How would your solution change if the input were an arbitrarily large integer?
learningObjectives: Apply integer division and modulus operations effectively.
